lesson.summary: Understand summary from first principles, with a small runnable example.

stage.name: Structural Patterns
stage.subtitle: Book chapter 10
stage.description: Adapter, bridge, composite, decorator, facade, proxy, and related structures.

payload.markdown: In this chapter, I looked at a few of the ways that classes and objects can be organized in a system. In particular, I focused on the principle that composition can be used to engender flexibility where inheritance fails. In both the Composite and Decorator patterns, inheritance is used to promote composition and to define a common interface that provides guarantees for client code.

blocks.text: In this chapter, I looked at a few of the ways that classes and objects can be organized in a system. In particular, I focused on the principle that composition can be used to engender flexibility where inheritance fails. In both the Composite and Decorator patterns, inheritance is used to promote composition and to define a common interface that provides guarantees for client code.

payload.markdown: You also saw delegation used effectively in these patterns. Finally, I looked at the simple but powerful Facade pattern. Facade is one of those patterns that many people have been using for years without having a name to give it. Facade lets you provide a clean point of entry to a tier or subsystem. In PHP, the Facade pattern is also used to create object wrappers that encapsulate blocks of procedural code.

items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Composition: Building classes from other objects instead of inheriting from them.
Inheritance: Deriving a class from a base class to reuse and specialise its behaviour.
Interfaces: A pure contract of method signatures with no implementation.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Behavioral Patterns: Patterns that distribute responsibility and coordinate behaviour.
